1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3.strategy: The flexible developing move: it guards d4 and e5 and leaves open where the dark-squared bishop will go until Black has shown how the other knight comes out. White keeps a solid centre and waits for Black to commit.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4.strategy: Goes for the central break at once, but Black takes the pawn and the knight has to recapture: the exchange removes Black's central pawn and leaves Black free to develop. White gets space and open lines, but no lasting pressure and nothing to aim at.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 closes it in. Black's bishop on e7 rules out Bg5, so the bishop takes the other good diagonal, where it eyes c7 and watches the centre. White keeps its options open for the rest of the pieces.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.cxd5.strategy: Releases the tension in the centre and heads for the exchange structure, in which White has the central pawn majority and Black the queenside one. Black's bishop on e7 has already ruled out Bg5, so White plays for a quiet, structural game, while Black's light-squared bishop is freed.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn offered by the central break and removes the d5 target. White has to win the pawn back with a piece or offer a gambit for it, while Black's pawn structure stays solid.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the other pawn and gives up the centre: Bxc4 recaptures with development and White keeps pawns on d4 and e4. Black stays solid but cramped, with the space and the initiative on White's side.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and hits e4, but White pushes the pawn on with tempo. After ...Nfd7 the knight cuts the queen off from d5, so cxd5 exd5 Nxd5 wins a pawn, and Black is cramped in any case.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4 dxe4 5.f3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Charousek Variation, Miladinovic Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4 dxe4 5.f3.strategy: A gambit: instead of recapturing, White hits the e4 pawn with the f-pawn to rebuild the centre and develop at speed. Black may keep the pawn, but the open lines and the lead in development keep the game balanced. Sound, though riskier than the simple recapture; the loosened king is the price.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4 dxe4 5.Nx.strategy: Recaptures at once and puts the knight on a strong central square, where it eyes the dark squares c5, d6 and f6. Black has given up the d5 pawn for it, so the tension on d5 is gone, and White keeps the pawns on c4 and d4 and the freer game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.e4 dxe4 5.Bg.strategy: Hangs the bishop: the bishop on e7 takes it, and nothing recaptures, because the knight on g1 does not cover g5. The usual pinning move of the Queen's Gambit is a blunder here.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Brings the knight out so that Black can castle next, and covers d5 and e4 again. With the bishop already on e7 the knight is shielded against the coming Bg5, so Black reaches the usual set-up without the pin.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 c6.strategy: Adds a second pawn to the support of d5, which makes the centre very solid. It costs a move that does not develop a piece, and the c8-bishop stays buried behind e6, so Black's game is safe but passive.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once and surrenders the centre. White regains it with a developing move and builds a broad pawn centre, while Black has not yet gained a tempo against the bishop. Playable, but it gives White the easier game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and aims it at the knight that defends d5 and guards e4: trading it would loosen Black's grip on the centre. White builds pressure on d5 while Black prepares a freeing break, the slow strategic game typical of this opening.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Harrwitz Attack
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.background: Peter Leko, usually a player of 1.e4, used it with White to beat Vladimir Kramnik in their 2004 World Championship match. Bobby Fischer played the line in game 14 of his 1972 match against Boris Spassky.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.strategy: Keeps the bishop outside the pawn chain, on the diagonal towards c7 and e5, and makes the knight exchanges that ease Black's game against a bishop on g5 less effective. It is a quieter, more manoeuvring way to fight for the centre, with more pieces kept on.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.e3.strategy: A solid, modest move that supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, but it shuts the queen's bishop in behind the pawn chain, the piece that usually needs a good square in this opening. White is safe and flexible, but Black has an easy game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.strategy: Castles and puts the king out of the centre. Nothing is threatened, since the queen guards c7, so Black can ignore the bishop and complete development. The king is safe and the rook comes towards the centre, ready for a freeing pawn break.

Offers to trade knights to ease the cramp: after the exchange the pawn recapturing on e4 hits the knight on f3. But that pawn is an advanced target that White can attack at once, the c8-bishop is still buried, and the bishop on f4 is placed to make this plan less effective.

Takes the pawn at once and gives up the centre. White regains it with a developing move, and the bishop on f4 already eyes c7, a square Black has to watch from now on. Playable, but it gives White the easier game.

Supports d4 and opens the diagonal of the king's bishop, so White can castle quickly behind a solid centre. The bishop on f4 stays outside the pawn chain instead of being shut in. Black must now decide how to challenge the centre.

Develops the queen to the b1-h7 diagonal, where it backs a later e4 break, while the bishop on f4 already controls the diagonal to c7. White delays e3 to keep the e-pawn flexible, at the price of leaving the king's bishop shut in for now.

Settles the tension in the centre: after ...exd5 White has the exchange structure with the bishop already outside the pawn chain on f4. Black's c8-bishop is freed, so Black has an easy game, and White plays for the long-term structure.

Strikes at d4 at once, the freeing break Black wants in this structure. Black accepts that the pawn structure may change, with an isolated pawn or hanging pawns, in return for open lines for the bishops and active pieces.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Harrwitz Attack, Fianchetto Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the light-squared bishop, the piece usually shut in behind e6, onto the long diagonal, where it will eye the centre and support d5. Black plans to free the problem piece and keeps the central pawns intact.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Harrwitz Attack, Orthodox Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.strategy: Reinforces d5 with a pawn, so White's pressure on it counts for little. The light-squared bishop stays boxed in behind e6, so Black accepts a patient, slightly passive game in which freeing the position takes time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Harrwitz Attack, Two Knights Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bf.strategy: Develops the second knight and covers e5, where the bishop on f4 points. The light-squared bishop stays shut in behind e6, so the set-up is solid but passive, and Black still has to find a way to free the position.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.strategy: Gets the king to safety and a rook towards the centre. The knight on f6 is shielded by the bishop on e7, so the bishop on g5 threatens nothing yet. Black keeps the solid structure and waits for White to show how the pressure will grow.

Asks the bishop at once what it intends. If White trades on f6, Black recaptures with the bishop and has the two bishops; if the bishop retreats, Black has put the question for free and the pawn on h6 gives the king some room.

Supports d5 solidly, but leaves the king in the centre and the light-squared bishop shut in, while the bishop on g5 stays aimed at the knight on f6. It is playable but slow, and it gives White time to finish development.

The solid, natural move: it supports d4 and c4, opens the f1-bishop and keeps the bishop on g5 pressing on the knight. White gets a space advantage and a slow, strategic game. Black, with ...c6 played, holds d5 firmly but still has the c8-bishop shut in behind the e6-pawn.

Clarifies the centre: after ...exd5 White gets the standard exchange structure with the bishop already on g5, the central majority facing Black's queenside one. Black's c8-bishop is free and the trade ...Nxd5 is possible, so White's edge is a long-term, structural one.

Puts the queen on the b1-h7 diagonal to back a later e4 break and keeps the f1-bishop's route flexible. The pawn on c4 stays loose behind the knight on c3, so Black can take it at once, but the set-up is sound and well known.

Develops the knight, supports the f6 knight and keeps d5 firmly defended. Black holds the tension in the centre and waits for White to commit the f1-bishop; Black can then capture on c4 and gain a tempo. The cost is a cramped game with the c8-bishop shut in.

Takes the pawn before White has committed the bishop to d3, so Bxc4 recaptures and develops the bishop in one move. Black surrenders the centre without winning a tempo in return and has to free the game by piece exchanges later. It is playable but gives White the easier game.

Castles at once instead of developing the second knight: the f6 knight is shielded by the bishop on e7, so the king can go to safety first. Black keeps the choice of knight square and the option to take on c4 once White's bishop has committed itself.

Keeps the bishop on the diagonal and the pressure on the knight on f6 instead of trading, so Black must decide how to deal with it. White holds the bishop for the fight against the centre and denies Black the bishop pair.

Trades the bishop for the knight that guards d5, but Black recaptures with the bishop and keeps the two bishops. White gives up its active bishop without a concrete gain, so this is the less ambitious choice.

Retreats along the other diagonal and keeps the bishop, but gives up the pin on f6, so ...h6 has cost Black nothing. White has less pressure than after Bh4, and Black can take on c4 at once. Playable, but the less ambitious retreat.
Castles into safety; the knight is shielded by the bishop on e7, so the bishop on h4 has no target. Black reaches a solid, balanced position and keeps a freeing break in the centre in reserve.

Adds a defender to the f6 knight, so that Bxf6 can be met by a knight recapture that keeps d5 guarded, and prepares castling. Black stays solid, but the knight on d7 blocks the queen's file and the c8-bishop is still shut in behind e6.

Takes the pawn at once and surrenders the centre while the king is still in the middle. Black has not gained the tempo that capturing after Bd3 would give, and White gets time to build a strong centre. Playable, but it gives White the easier game.

Recaptures with the bishop, keeping the pawn structure intact and the two bishops. The bishop on f6 looks at the centre, and the d5 pawn is still comfortably defended. White has the trade but no lasting pressure, and Black is solid.

Recaptures with the pawn instead of the bishop: the structure is ruined, with doubled f-pawns and an isolated h-pawn. The open g-file and the bishop pair are no compensation for a long-term weakness that White can aim at.
Counterattacks the c4 pawn instead of recapturing, but loses a piece: White's bishop takes on e7, the queen recaptures, and White is a knight up for a pawn.

Solidly supports d4 and the centre and opens the way for the f1-bishop and castling. The g5-bishop stays to press on the f6-knight, which the e7-bishop shields for now. White settles for a long manoeuvring game in which the extra space matters.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Miles Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bg.strategy: Develops the queen to the b1-h7 diagonal, where it guards c4 and backs a later e4 break. White keeps the e-pawn flexible, at the price of slower development of the kingside pieces.

Releases the tension and heads for the exchange structure: after ...exd5 White keeps the bishop on g5 pressing on f6 and has the central majority. Black's c8-bishop is freed and ...Nxd5 is possible, so this gives Black easier play than the quiet build-up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.e3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Three Knights Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.e3.strategy: Castles before White has shown a plan. The king is safe and the rook comes towards the centre, so Black can wait. The standing worry is the c8-bishop shut in behind e6, freed later by a ...c5 break or by taking on c4 once White's bishop has committed itself.

The freeing break: Black strikes at d4 at once to open lines for the pieces, instead of waiting behind the e6 pawn. The price is a changed pawn structure, typically an isolated or hanging pawn, which active piece play has to justify.

Develops the second knight, supports the f6 knight and keeps d5 firmly guarded, ready to castle. Black waits for White to commit the f1-bishop, since capturing on c4 after Bd3 gains a tempo. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind e6.

Avoids the usual pin on f6 and prepares the queen's bishop for b2, where it supports the centre. The b3 pawn also firms up c4, so Black's capture there would only help White build a broad centre. A restrained set-up with a long game ahead.

Develops the bishop to its natural diagonal, aimed at the kingside, so that White can castle quickly. It allows ...dxc4, which gains a tempo against the bishop but gives up the centre, so White keeps the freer game.

Places the queen on the b1-h7 diagonal to back an e4 break and keep the set-up flexible. It delays the development of the king's bishop, and the pawn on c4 stays to be regained by a piece if Black takes it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.e3.name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Be7 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.e3.strategy: Mirrors White's plan and gives the light-squared bishop a diagonal, instead of leaving it as the passive piece behind the e6 pawn. Black stays compact and lets the bishop wait for the centre to open.

Strikes at the centre at once, before the bishop on b2 is in place: Black challenges d4 and aims to trade pawns so that the pieces get room. The price may be an isolated or hanging pawn, which active piece play has to justify.

Takes the pawn, but the recapture with the b-pawn gives White a broad pawn centre with its pieces behind it. Black has given up the central tension and has little to show for it; playable, but it makes White's plan easier.
